body: Saturday, June 27 2026 — Macro · Sectors · Flows · Crypto

Macro Stance: The Fed under Chair Kevin Warsh is confronting inflation that has hit a 3-year high. Markets are now pricing a rate hold in July with a hike expected in September. Kashkari stated publicly that the Fed may have to raise rates this year. The 2Y yield at 4.07% (prior close) is rising (+8 bps vs 4W) reflecting front-end repricing, while the 10Y at 4.45% is unchanged vs 4W, compressing the curve to +31 bps — positive but still flat by historical standards. VIX at 18.89 is elevated (+16%), and the S&P 500 has pulled back ~2.2% over four weeks. The dollar has rallied to a 13-month high.

New / Most Important: This week's signal cluster is structurally significant: the U.S. appears to be entering a rate HIKE cycle for the first time since 2023, with multiple Fed officials and market pricing converging on this view. Trump reportedly eased pressure on Warsh as inflation topped 4%, suggesting political acquiescence to tightening — a major shift from prior rhetoric. The Nasdaq slumped over 4.5% for the week as high-flying AI stocks bled, while corporate profits are surging per Axios. Jeremy Grantham called this "the most expensive market in American history." A "mega rotation" out of tech into value/small-caps is underway — the Russell 2000 is up 3% vs 4W while Nasdaq 100 is down 1.8%, a nearly 5% divergence in relative terms. Bond traders trimmed some hike bets after one benign inflation print, but the hawks clearly dominate the conversation. The richest 20% are the only ones powering the economy per a top economist, making asset prices a macro vulnerability in a tightening regime.

Playbook ✓: Dollar strength following hawkish Fed repricing is textbook. Tech underperformance in a rising-rate environment follows the duration playbook perfectly.  |  ⚠️ Divergence: The structural break here is that we may be witnessing a regime change from "higher for longer" to an outright hiking cycle in 2026 — something consensus had fully abandoned as recently as Q1. This is happening while the AI capex boom is simultaneously driving corporate profits AND contributing to inflationary pressure through energy demand and wage competition — a supply-side inflation impulse that rate hikes may struggle to contain. The fact that only the top 20% of earners are powering consumption means the transmission mechanism of rate hikes is highly asymmetric: it will crush housing and small business credit long before it touches the wealth-effect-driven spending of the affluent. Meanwhile, the Russell/Nasdaq rotation suggests capital is already fleeing duration-sensitive mega-cap tech for domestically-oriented small-caps — a flow pattern typically associated with late-cycle positioning, not early-cycle optimism. The political dimension is critical: Trump acquiescing to Warsh's hawkishness ahead of what may be an election year signals either genuine inflation panic in the White House or a strategic gambit to get the pain over with early.

Macro Stance: The ECB raised rates for the first time since 2023 this past week, a landmark reversal. Schnabel stated rates need to rise further to return inflation to 2%. Lane warned inflation could stay high even with a peace deal. The euro sank to a one-year low despite the hike, driven by falling oil prices easing urgency and divergent Fed-ECB signaling dynamics.

New / Most Important: The ECB's rate hike is the structural headline. This is the first hike since the 2022-2023 tightening cycle and marks a definitive end to any easing hopes. Eurozone consumer inflation expectations cooled to 3.5% per the ECB's own survey — creating a tension between hawkish policy and softening expectations. The euro's weakness despite a hike is notable: the currency fell to its lowest 2026 level near 1.13 against the surging dollar, suggesting capital flows are overwhelmingly favoring the U.S. in a twin-hike environment. Falling oil prices (WTI down 22% over 4W) should theoretically provide relief on energy-driven inflation, but the ECB is clearly looking through this.

Playbook ✓: Hawkish ECB language aligns with above-target inflation. Euro weakness vs. a stronger dollar is standard rate-differential mechanics.  |  ⚠️ Divergence: The ECB hiking while oil collapses 22% is a genuinely unusual policy choice. Historically, the ECB has been the most energy-price-sensitive major central bank, and a deflationary oil shock of this magnitude would normally buy them room to pause. That they're hiking anyway suggests either deep concern about services inflation persistence or a credibility-driven move to anchor expectations after the consumer survey showed 3.5% — still well above target. The euro falling on a hike is a classic "sell the fact" but may also reflect capital outflows from Europe into higher-yielding U.S. assets, which would be a negative feedback loop: weaker euro → imported inflation → more hikes needed → more growth damage.

Macro Stance: The PBOC is rebuilding its operating framework rather than cutting. Loan prime rates were held for a 13th month in June (Reuters, [Jun 21]), the 1-year LPR at 3.0% (Mitrade, [Jun 21]), and the bank now plans an overnight reverse repo as the next stage of its policy shift (Bloomberg, [Jun 25]), with a survey pointing to a new overnight rate of 1.35% ([Jun 25]). StanChart sees tightening as unlikely (Bloomberg, [Jun 25]): the bias is easing, but the tool is liquidity, not price. The yuan fixing was weakened for a fourth session as the dollar advanced (Bloomberg, [Jun 23]): a managed drift lower against a dollar at 13-month highs, while the ECB openly calls the yuan undervalued (Reuters, [Jun 22]); T. Rowe Price sees it falling 1%-2% by year-end (TradingView, [Jun 26]). Prices are split. May CPI rose only 1.2% and missed expectations (China Daily, [Jun 10]), while factory-gate inflation hit a near four-year high on Iran-war input costs and the AI boom (Reuters, [Jun 9]).

PMIs & Activity: The official manufacturing PMI stalled at 50 in May (Reuters, [May 30]) with factory orders contracting (Wood Central, [Jun 1]), and the non-manufacturing gauge was barely positive at 50.1 (Macau Business, [May 31]). Private surveys were firmer, with services at 54.4 (TradingView, [Jun 2]). The hard data confirm a two-speed economy. Industrial output growth quickened to 4.5% in May (China Daily, [Jun 16]), but retail sales fell 0.6%, the first drop in over three years (Il Sole 24 Ore, [Jun 15]), and fixed-asset investment was down 4.1% in the first five months (Macau Business, [Jun 16]). Industrial profits rose 18.8% in January–May (WSJ, [Jun 26]), but the May gain dipped in a sign of weakness (Bloomberg, [Jun 26]): even the export engine is losing some margin.

Credit Impulse: Total social financing grew 7.7% in May (CGTN, [Jun 12]) and topped forecasts (Bloomberg, [Jun 12]), but new loans missed as the property slump curbed demand (Reuters, [Jun 12]). The beat is government-bond issuance; private credit demand is still contracting. The PBOC is now urging banks to boost lending because demand remains weak, according to sources (Reuters, [Jun 26]). That is the key tell: the constraint on the credit impulse is borrower demand, not bank liquidity. Bloomberg notes the tilt from loans to bonds ([Jun 17]), and household deleveraging continues (SCMP, [Jun 15]) against a $300 billion pile of bad consumer debt (Bloomberg, [Jun 17]). Read: the headline impulse is flat-to-positive, but the household and private-firm impulse is still negative, which is why output does not convert into consumption.

Property: New home prices fell at a faster pace in May (Reuters, [Jun 15]), a setback to the revival story, even as first-tier new home prices rose for a third month (SCMP, [Jun 16]) and top-city resale prices extended their rebound (Caixin, [Jun 17]). Real-estate investment fell 16.2% y/y in January–May (GMK Center, [Jun 18]). This week the stress resurfaced at the developer level: Beijing land sales plunged 66% as developers chase only "safe" prime plots (Caixin, [Jun 25]), and the Evergrande Property Services stake sale collapsed, sending its shares down 24% (Caixin, [Jun 26]). Bloomberg describes steel entering a long plateau after the property crash ([Jun 21]).

Fiscal, Policy & Trade: The fiscal signal is the surprise. Beijing narrowed its cumulative deficit for the first time since 2023 (Bloomberg, [Jun 22]), against a 2026 deficit ratio of around 4% (China Daily, [Jun 20]). A third batch of 62.5 billion yuan for consumer-goods trade-ins was allocated (Global Times, [Jun 26]): targeted support, small relative to the retail contraction. Exports jumped 19.4% in May (AP, [Jun 9]) and shipments to the US grew 35% (CNBC, [Jun 8]). Brussels is hardening its stance as trade talks reopen (POLITICO.eu, [Jun 26]) and readying tariffs on Chinese plug-in hybrids (CnEVPost, [Jun 20]). Beijing put 10 US firms, including MP Materials and USA Rare Earth, on its export-control list in response to the Pentagon blacklist (Reuters, [Jun 22]), and the 55% tariff on Australian beef is now in force (Australian Rural & Regional News, [Jun 22]).

Markets & Flows: Onshore and offshore have decoupled. Mainland stocks hit a 4-1/2-year high (TradingView, [Jun 22]), led by AI names on demand optimism and policy support (Bloomberg, [Jun 21]). Hong Kong is the opposite: the HSCEI entered a technical bear market (finance.biggo.com, [Jun 23]), Bloomberg ties the slide to spending woes ([Jun 23]), and the Hang Seng capped its worst week in over a year amid a tech sell-off (SCMP, [Jun 26]). The securities regulator also ordered curbs on cross-border swaps (Business Times, [Jun 26]), tightening the offshore channel.

New / Most Important: The PBOC asking banks to lend more is an admission that liquidity is not the binding constraint. With new loans missing, household deleveraging and the first fiscal-gap cutback since 2023, the credit impulse that matters for the real economy is not turning. Moral suasion does not create borrowers. That leaves growth leaning on exports, just as Europe prepares trade defences.

Playbook ✓: Property drag, weak consumption, LPR on hold and a managed yuan drift lower are all on script.  |  ⚠️ Divergence: The consensus expected a mid-year stimulus pivot; instead the credit impulse outside government bonds is negative and the fiscal impulse is narrowing. China is therefore exporting its excess supply rather than absorbing it at home. The transmission runs through three channels. European exporters face a widening bilateral deficit and a weak yuan just as the EU moves on tariffs. Bulk-commodity demand tied to construction is fading, with the steel plateau and an investment slump that hit AUD alongside the beef tariff. And global goods disinflation is the channel Pimco expects to support EM bonds (Bloomberg, [Jun 23]). A real turn needs loan growth, not bond issuance, to re-accelerate; until it does, rallies in Hong Kong are flows, not fundamentals.

Macro Stance: The BOJ has hiked rates, yet the yen continues to fall — the definitive "buy the rumor, sell the fact" dynamic. Multiple BOJ members called for faster hikes in the latest summary. A hawkish dissenter linked to PM Takaichi pushed for hikes once every few months. An ex-BOJ policymaker warned a Fed hike could push yen to 165. Japan continues to issue intervention warnings that the market is ignoring.

New / Most Important: The structural story here is the failure of rate hikes to support the currency. This is a textbook capital-flow problem: Japan's rate differential with the U.S. is so extreme that even BOJ tightening cannot overcome the carry trade pull. The Takaichi-linked dissenter calling for faster hikes hints at political pressure to defend the yen, but the BOJ is in a bind — aggressive hiking risks crashing JGBs and the domestic mortgage market. The feed explicitly says "the yen got its hike; Tokyo still has to do the rest" — meaning fiscal and structural reform is needed, not just monetary policy. If the Fed actually hikes in September, the yen could face another leg down regardless of BOJ actions.

Playbook ✓: BOJ hawkishness amid above-target inflation is on script.  |  ⚠️ Divergence: The yen falling despite a hike is the divergence. Japan is trapped: the only way to truly defend the yen is to sell U.S. Treasuries (their largest reserve asset), which would push U.S. yields higher and tighten global financial conditions — a nuclear option with systemic consequences. Verbal intervention has lost all credibility.

Macro Stance: The RBA held rates at its latest meeting, providing near-term relief. However, Deputy Governor Hauser stated inflation "remains far too high" and the bank still has "work to do." Underlying inflation remains sticky even as headline cooled. Bond traders are not ruling out a fourth rate rise.

New / Most Important: The RBA hold was the key event. But the hawkish language surrounding it keeps the door wide open — this is an RBA that is clearly uncomfortable with its inflation trajectory. The oil collapse (-22%) should provide commodity-driven disinflation relief and housing is already cooling — home prices flatlined in May and Bloomberg warns they may fall up to 8% — but services inflation is the binding constraint.  |  Playbook ✓: Hold-with-hawkish-bias is consensus.  |  ⚠️ Divergence: None today — the RBA is playing it exactly by the book.

Macro Stance: The RPP is in wait mode (Parkiet, [Jun 25]; wGospodarce, [Jun 23]) and the labour data are the argument for staying there: Bankier.pl noted employment is still falling while pay grows slowly, and said the figures should discourage the RPP from discussing hikes [Jun 22], after NBP revealed a vote for a hike at the last meeting (Tysol.pl, [Jun 22]). The NBP survey has inflation under control but cuts uncertain (Parkiet, [Jun 24]). Prices are easing at the shelf, with food inflation clearly weakening (CEO Magazyn, [Jun 19]), but Rzeczpospolita notes Polish price levels have converged from 58% to 73% of the EU average in a decade [Jun 27]. The supply side is the bright spot: Business Insider Polska says the wave of defence orders is a stimulus Poland has never had [Jun 27], while pb.pl reports credit growth at its fastest in 14 years as part of a global cycle [Jun 23]. Against that, construction slowed despite EU billions (Rzeczpospolita, [Jun 22]) and retail sales missed (Bankier.pl, [Jun 22]). Poland is still cast as the outlier dove in a world of hawks, but the feed supports a hold with a hawkish minority, not easing.

Markets: The week closed with a correction: Inwestycje.pl has the WIG20 lower on Friday with Kęty and Żabka against the market [Jun 26], StockWatch.pl tying it to a global sell-off with Allegro, Kęty, PGE and Text in play [Jun 26]. The card now carries Friday's closes. EPOL at 38.27 is down 3.7% on the week and 5.7% over four weeks. KGHM at 327.75 is still 10.3% lower on the week after Wednesday's 7.5% drop (wnp.pl, [Jun 24]). Orlen at 123.46 (-2.3% 1W, -12.6% 4W) and PGE at 9.6 (-1.9% 1W, -11.1% 4W) gave back Thursday's energy rebound. Allegro at 37.19 lost 5.7% on the week despite the buyback, though it is still up 8.7% over four weeks; CD Projekt at 217.4 (-3.0% 1W) confirmed the loss of 220 zł (CrypS.pl, [Jun 26]); LPP at 18310 is 16.4% below its level four weeks ago; PKO at 103.62 and Pekao at 228.8 are off 1.6% and 2.8%; Dino at 28.98 is roughly flat on the week. FX held: USD/PLN at 3.7661 (+1.4% 1W, +3.9% 4W) and EUR/PLN at 4.2788 (+0.6% 1W, +1.3% 4W), with the euro below 4.30 zł (Bankier.pl, [Jun 26]) and pb.pl seeing a weaker dollar, a stable zloty and falling bond yields [Jun 26]. The bond story is cost: Parkiet reports Treasury debt galloping with servicing costs up almost 30% [Jun 25], and July retail bonds pay up to 5.65% (Subiektywnie o finansach, [Jun 24]).

Fiscal & Politics: Bankier.pl flags an accumulation of state spending ahead, with billions for nuclear and the CPK airport against the backdrop of an EU procedure [Jun 27]; economists already appealed for caution on borrowing given the pile-up of costly investments (Newseria BIZNES, [Jun 24]). The arithmetic is stark: debt rose 46.8 bn zł in a month (Gazeta Prawna, [Jun 22]) and wPolityce.pl puts it at 1.5 bn zł a day in May 2026 against 0.9 bn zł a day in 2025 [Jun 26]. On the windfall tax, the Senate added a safety valve after a 74% rate for oil firms was raised (Wyborcza.biz, [Jun 26]). Revenue measures keep coming: alcohol and sugar levies for healthcare (Bloomberg, [Jun 24]) and a new tax from 2027 after the president blocked raises (Gazeta Prawna, [Jun 25]). The CHF law passed the Senate unamended (Gazeta Prawna, [Jun 25]) and CHF24 describes automatic suspension of instalments once a case is filed, with a real chance of the president's signature [Jun 27].

Corporate & Sectors: Orlen is raising prices again: wholesale fuel went up as crude rose (Bankier.pl, [Jun 26]) and station prices rise from Saturday (Rzeczpospolita, [Jun 27]), while the company confirmed two more Naftogaz agreements (Inwestycje.pl, [Jun 25]) and the Cerisa North Sea investment decision (StockWatch.pl, [Jun 25]). The PGE-Enea-Orlen-Tauron letter of intent on Ukrainian energy reconstruction stands (StockWatch.pl, [Jun 26]), and Rzeczpospolita argues east-west integration runs through energy [Jun 27]. Allegro's buyback runs at up to 42 mln shares and a maximum 45 zł (StockWatch.pl, [Jun 26]). Dino's labour problem deepened: unions went to prosecutors (DlaHandlu.pl, [Jun 26]) and FXMAG reports staff overwhelmed by workloads [Jun 27]. Energy: the heatwave is hitting generation and may lift power prices (Interia Biznes, [Jun 27]) after spot hit 1442 zł per MWh (wnp.pl, [Jun 25]). Taiwan plans chip and EV plants in Poland (The Diplomat, [Jun 26]).

Geopolitics & Security: The Guardian reports NATO leaders fear they can no longer rely on US help if Russia attacks [Jun 27], a day after it reported Russia preparing a possible provocation in the Baltics or Poland [Jun 26]. Sikorski repeated that Russia may stage a false flag to justify an attack on NATO (The New Voice of Ukraine, [Jun 27]), and Firstpost framed the aim as testing NATO unity [Jun 27]. Warsaw's answer is capacity: Europe's largest anti-drone system (DW, [Jun 26]) and the defence-order stimulus. BGK entered the Ukraine reconstruction fund with 15 mln euro, rising to as much as 500 mln (Rzeczpospolita, [Jun 26]).

New / Most Important: The cost of money for the state is now the headline risk: servicing costs up almost 30%, debt at 1.5 bn zł a day and a spending pile-up for nuclear and CPK that Bankier.pl explicitly links to an EU procedure. That is why the zloty is weak at a hold-rate NBP and why the windfall tax is being pushed toward 74%. Private credit at a 14-year high and record defence orders say the economy can take it; the bond market says the budget cannot for long.  |  Playbook ✓: Hold, not cut; lean into banks on credit growth and the CHF endgame, keep energy and KGHM underweight through the tax debate, and fund it from LPP and Allegro, where the four-week drawdown and the buyback have already done the work.  |  ⚠️ Divergence: Credit growth at a 14-year high while employment falls; falling POLGB yields against a 30% rise in servicing costs; NATO doubts about US backing in the same week Poland is called the alliance's most powerful fortress (Forsal.pl, [Jun 25]).

Macro Stance: Brazil's central bank is signaling caution on inflation per this week's feed. In a world where the Fed and ECB are both hiking, EM central banks that need to ease face impossible choices. Dollar strength past 1,545 won (Korea proxy) confirms broad EM FX pressure.  |  New / Most Important: BCB hawkish signaling amid a commodity price collapse (oil -22%) is notable — suggests domestic demand-driven inflation, not imported.  |  Playbook ✓: EM tightening in response to USD strength is standard.  |  ⚠️ Divergence: None — EM pain from synchronized DM hiking is the consensus call playing out.

Narrative: A "mega rotation" out of tech took the Nasdaq 100 down 4.5% on the week: with inflation at a 3-year high, a September hike priced and valuations stretched, the market is repricing duration, and long-duration software multiples are the first to compress.

Reported: BlackBerry beat on Q1 earnings and the stock climbed 20% on an upbeat outlook (TradingView, [Jun 26]), with its CEO saying Alloy Kore could unlock higher software revenue (Stocktwits, [Jun 26]). TD SYNNEX beat on broad-based growth and Hyve strength (Yahoo Finance, [Jun 26]).

EPS Upside Watch: Oracle — a $638 billion AI backlog points to revenue the share price does not yet reflect (24/7 Wall St., [Jun 23]). Fair Isaac, after raising its revenue guidance to $2.45 billion (TIKR.com, [Jun 25]).

⚡ Breaking Convention: AI stocks bled even as corporate profits surged: the sell-off is a rates and valuation call, not an earnings one. Fortune argues the AI boom will first surge in a blow-off phase before the bubble pops — so bears on the theme may be early.

Narrative: Alphabet replacing Verizon in the Dow crowns the new-economy giants over legacy telco, and PwC sees global entertainment and media advertising revenues reaching US$1.4 trillion in 2030 (PwC, [Jun 22]), but near term the driver is rates, with the 10Y at 4.45% capping long-duration platform names.
Reported: No major reports this week.
EPS Upside Watch: Take-Two — an analyst says GTA VI could transform earnings (Benzinga, [Jun 24]). Alphabet, where Wall Street keeps raising its target while the stock slips (TIKR.com, [Jun 21]).

⚡ Breaking Convention: Dow inclusion forces index-tracking flows into Alphabet just as active managers rotate out of mega-cap tech — forced buying that could open a relative-performance wedge between it and other tech names.

Narrative: A Fed leaning toward a September hike keeps net interest income high even with the 10Y-2Y spread at a thin +31 bps, the Russell 2000's ↑3.0% points to regional-bank participation in the rotation, and bond traders repricing the curve support trading revenue.

Reported: Jefferies dropped 2% as an earnings miss overshadowed record banking revenue (TradingView, [Jun 25]). Judo Capital cut FY26 profit guidance after three loans went bad (Stocks Down Under, [Jun 25]). Banca Ifis cut profit guidance after launching the sale of its NPL business (MarketScreener, [Jun 26]).

EPS Upside Watch: The biggest US banks, which aced the Fed's 2026 stress test (Global Finance Magazine, [Jun 25]). RHB Bank, whose 2Q profit is seen improving on better margins and treasury income (The Edge Malaysia, [Jun 26]).
⚡ Breaking Convention: None today — financials benefiting from a hawkish Fed is on-script.

Narrative: WTI at $69.23 is down 22.1% in four weeks as US drillers add rigs for a fourth straight week into the slide and falling Chinese oil imports take out the demand leg; tanker earnings plunged by $200,000 as more ships return to Hormuz (Bloomberg.com, [Jun 26]).
Reported: Worley, the energy and resources engineering contractor, faces an investor trust crisis after a fresh profit warning (AFR, [Jun 25]).
EPS Upside Watch: Indian refiner-marketers BPCL and IOC — JP Morgan says falling crude prices will boost their marketing margins (The New Indian Express, [Jun 22]).

⚡ Breaking Convention: Solar beating coal for the first time is a structural milestone: if solar becomes the marginal electron, the long-term demand ceiling for coal and potentially natural gas shifts lower, and sector leadership may rotate from upstream E&P to utilities and renewables infrastructure for years.

Narrative: The Russell 2000's ↑3.0% rotation favours domestic industrials, but the PMIs give a split read — the June flash put US manufacturing at a 4-year high while factory jobs are at their lowest since 2020 and German business activity is at an 18-month low — so next week's ISM manufacturing print is the test (CMC Markets, [Jun 26]).

Reported: FedEx fell 6% despite beating revenue and earnings estimates (TIKR.com, [Jun 24]), while FedEx Freight's first report beat estimates and the stock did not move (Barron's, [Jun 26]). Heathrow warned on profit amid falling traffic and rising costs (The Times, [Jun 26]).

EPS Upside Watch: Bloom Energy — the stock could be worth $920 after the Oracle deal expansion (TIKR.com, [Jun 26]). Airlines, whose earnings are set for takeoff even if the stocks lag (Barron's, [Jun 26]).
⚡ Breaking Convention: None today.

Narrative: With inflation at a 3-year high and only the richest 20% powering the economy, rate-hike bets and falling equity prices create a negative wealth effect that leaves middle-income discretionary demand exposed, as Olive Garden shows.

Reported: Darden beat on earnings but Olive Garden growth weakened (CNBC, [Jun 25]), and it forecast annual profit below estimates on higher costs (BNN Bloomberg, [Jun 25]). H&M's profit missed estimates (The Business of Fashion, [Jun 25]). Halfords rose 13% as profit beat forecasts and margins hit a decade high (Yahoo Finance UK, [Jun 25]).

EPS Upside Watch: Nike — its looming report fuels turnaround optimism (Investor's Business Daily, [Jun 26]) against low expectations (TradingKey, [Jun 26]). Coursera, on surging earnings estimates (Yahoo Finance, [Jun 26]).
⚡ Breaking Convention: None today.
Narrative: Staples are the classic defensive beneficiary of a rising-rate, falling-equity tape, and falling oil eases input and freight costs.

Reported: McCormick beat Q2 estimates as organic sales grew (TradingView, [Jun 25]). Couche-Tard's profit rose on increased same-store sales (WSJ, [Jun 22]), with its CEO citing the "best performance in years" in the US (C-Store Dive, [Jun 24]). Procter & Gamble maintained guidance amid steady demand (International Business Times Australia, [Jun 24]).
EPS Upside Watch: None flagged.
⚡ Breaking Convention: None today.

Narrative: Healthcare is a natural destination for the rotation out of tech, pairing defensive earnings with secular growth in obesity and diabetes treatment as rate-hike bets build — Eli Lilly soared — while Medtronic's tariff disclosures are a headwind for medtech.

Reported: Johnson & Johnson raised its outlook while pushing U.S. investments, and the shares climbed (International Business Times Australia, [Jun 24]). Beximco Pharma's nine-month profit jumped to Tk704cr (The Business Standard, [Jun 24]).

EPS Upside Watch: IDEXX, after raising its 2026 EPS outlook to $15 (TIKR.com, [Jun 25]). Dr Reddy's — Nomura sees 35% upside after its strategic consumer-health pivot (The Financial Express, [Jun 23]).
⚡ Breaking Convention: Not all of the bid is defensive: Palvella Therapeutics' 620% rally followed by insider selling points to speculative froth in rare-disease biotech.

Narrative: Broad commodity deflation is crushing materials: gold at $4,079 (↓9.3%) is unwinding on hike bets with the dollar at a 13-month high, and copper, down 4.0% in four weeks, trades as an AI data-centre and grid metal tracking the tech rout. The construction side hinges on China, where real-estate investment fell 16.2% y/y in January–May.

Reported: Evonik raised guidance on higher prices and cost reductions (WSJ, [Jun 26]). Synthomer beat Q2 expectations and its shares surged 8% (Global Banking & Finance Review, [Jun 22]). Satellite Chemical hit limit-up on a forecast that first-half net profit will surge over 118% to a record (finance.biggo.com, [Jun 23]).
EPS Upside Watch: Barrick — ChartMill flags 121% EPS growth (ChartMill, [Jun 22]).

⚡ Breaking Convention: Chemicals are pricing through the slump: Evonik raised guidance on higher prices and cost cuts and Satellite Chemical forecasts a record first half, so the commodity deflation hitting miners is not reaching every chemical margin.

Narrative: Rate-hike expectations are the worst backdrop for REITs: the 2Y at 4.07% (+8 bps vs 4W) tightens commercial property financing even as mortgage rates ended the week at lows (Mortgage News Daily, [Jun 26]).

Reported: KB Home met Q2 earnings estimates (Yahoo Finance, [Jun 23]) on lower revenue as the housing market stays difficult (WSJ, [Jun 23]), leaving a scale-versus-execution debate (HousingWire, [Jun 25]). UK homebuilder Berkeley called for a tax and regulatory rethink after a 15% profit fall (Reuters, [Jun 24]).
EPS Upside Watch: None flagged.
⚡ Breaking Convention: None today.

Narrative: AI data-centre power demand is the structural bid, but September hike bets lift the discount rate on bond-proxy cash flows, and a bill in Congress would make tech companies pay data-centre energy costs (CNBC, [Jun 24]).
Reported: UK multi-utility supplier Telecom Plus fell 25% on a profit warning and a dividend cut (Sharecast.com, [Jun 23]).
EPS Upside Watch: None flagged.

⚡ Breaking Convention: AI data-centre demand meeting solar-first generation could make select utilities the best risk-adjusted AI plays — cheaper power, growing demand, regulated returns — a contrarian long against hyperscaler capex names.

Narrative: China is the driver — BMW's 1-3% profit margin is called a wake-up call for the auto industry in the face of Chinese competition (Yahoo Finance, [Jun 26]) — and an ECB hike plus euro weakness complete a triple headwind, with OEMs pooling software code to "catch China".

Reported: Porsche's CEO stuck to his targets on the road to recovery (Reuters, [Jun 22]). Volkswagen plans up to 100,000 job cuts, saying the risk situation has never been so high (New York Post, [Jun 26]).
EPS Upside Watch: Mercedes — it is starting talks with workers on additional savings (Automotive News, [Jun 22]), a cost lever for margins if volumes hold.

Narrative: The AI picks-and-shovels thesis is intact and the earnings power is real, but a US chipmaker sell-off pushed key indices to a weekly loss (Yahoo Finance Singapore, [Jun 26]), so AI capex conviction now trades against rate-hike risk as valuations reprice with broader tech.
